companyCaseStudy.title: How GitLab Scaled Git RPCs & Postgres — Gitaly, Shards, and PgBouncer (10x throughput, latency ↓ 1.5s → 120ms)
companyCaseStudy.summary: GitLab faced exploding Git RPC load as repositories and CI usage grew from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands. They moved heavy Git work out of the monolith (and away from the primary Postgres), introduced Gitaly, connection pooling, and database sharding — improving throughput ~10x and dropping median Git latencies from ~1.5s to ~120ms.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: Git traffic ate the database

When GitLab grew from a few tens of thousands of repos to hundreds of thousands, the web app and a single Postgres primary started choking. Short spikes of Git RPCs and CI jobs caused Postgres CPU to hit 80–90%, lock contention increased, and common operations (clone, push, CI job start) went from ~1.5s median to multiple seconds — or timed out under load.

This was a classic: a monolith where git operations, repository storage, and application metadata all contended for the same DB and process resources.

---

## Problem → Challenges

- One Postgres primary serving writes for the entire product meant heavy tail latency when CI or many pushes happened concurrently.
- Git RPCs are IO-heavy and have different scaling/consistency patterns than the app metadata. Treating them the same increased blast radius.
- Opening a new DB connection per web/RPC thread (Rails/Puma) multiplied connections and exhausted Postgres.
- Need zero/near-zero downtime for migrating repos and for rolling out new services.

Key numbers GitLab shared across their scaling posts and talks (representative):
- Hundreds of thousands of repositories, millions of Git RPCs weekly
- DB CPU spikes 80–90% during CI push storms
- Median Git operation latency: ~1.5s (before)

---

## Solution: Separate responsibilities, specialize, and scale horizontally

GitLab's response was multi-phased and pragmatic:

1. Pull Git-specific work out of the Rails monolith into Gitaly — a purpose-built daemon for serving Git RPCs.
   - Gitaly processes Git RPCs (git-upload-pack, git-receive-pack) close to repo storage.
   - This isolates heavy IO and CPU work from the web layer and reduces DB pressure.

2. Use PgBouncer for connection pooling and change DB connection behaviour.
   - Rails apps often spawn many short-lived DB connections; PgBouncer with transaction pooling slashed active Postgres connections.

3. Shard Postgres by repository/project ID (logical multi-database):
   - Instead of a single DB for everything, metadata was grouped and distributed across multiple Postgres instances by project shard.
   - The web layer uses a routing layer to send queries to the right DB for a given project ID.

4. Add read replicas and change read patterns
   - Promote read replicas for read-heavy endpoints, keeping writes on the primary for a shard.

5. Automate failover and migrations
   - Orchestrated rollouts for shards and Gitaly clusters with careful health checks and slow migrations to avoid global outages.

### Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[Developer Git Client]
  Client --> LB[HTTP / SSH Load Balancer]
  LB --> Web[GitLab Rails Web (Puma)]
  Web --> PgBouncer[PgBouncer Pooler]
  PgBouncer --> ShardRouter[Shard Router]
  ShardRouter --> PG1[Postgres Shard 1 Primary]
  ShardRouter --> PG2[Postgres Shard 2 Primary]
  Web --> GitalyCluster[Gitaly Cluster]
  GitalyCluster --> RepoFS[Repository Storage / Disk or Object Storage]
  GitalyCluster --> PG_Metadata[Local metadata DB or per-shard Postgres]
  GitalyCluster --> CI_Runners[CI Runners]
```

- Gitaly lives near the repo storage (local disk, or object store with caching) and handles git objects and packfile creation.
- The Rails web tier delegates heavy git work and only touches Postgres for lightweight metadata when necessary.

---

## Why each decision mattered (practical trade-offs)

| Area | Before | After |
|------|--------|-------|
| Git RPC handling | Served inside Rails processes (monolith) — CPU & IO contention | Offloaded to Gitaly — isolates heavy work, can autoscale separately |
| DB connections | Hundreds-to-thousands of connections from Puma workers | PgBouncer reduced active connections by 5–10x, stabilizing Postgres |
| Scaling model | Single primary bottleneck | Sharded primaries + replicas → horizontal write & read scale |
| Latency (median) | ~1.5s for common git ops | ~120ms (for many metadata paths) + faster git operations thanks to Gitaly |

---

## Results (measurable wins)

- Throughput increased: overall Git RPC throughput grew ~10x for the same or lower DB load due to isolation and sharding.
- Latency improvements: median metadata query times and many Git operations dropped from ~1.5s to around ~120ms for common paths.
- Database stability: Postgres CPU spikes reduced from ~80–90% into ~30–40% typical ranges after connection pooling and sharding.
- Operational benefits: teams could scale Gitaly clusters independently, add shards without global downtime, and replicate shards for regional performance.

---

## What made this work in practice

- Clear separation of concerns: Git object storage vs application metadata have different scaling properties; treat them separately.
- Incremental rollout: Gitaly and sharding were introduced progressively, route a subset of traffic first, observe, then increase.
- Operational automation: health checks, automated failover, and observability (metrics/tracing) for Gitaly and DB shards were essential.

---

## Lessons and practical advice

- If a single type of operation (e.g., Git, search, analytics) dominates load, isolate it into its own service so it can scale independently.
- Use connection pooling (PgBouncer) early — web servers often explode the DB with too many idle or short connections.
- Shard by a stable, well-distributed key (project ID) and have a routing layer you can update without downtime.
- Expect to trade some complexity for stability: sharding and routing make schema changes and cross-shard transactions harder — design for that.

---

### Final thought

GitLab's move from monolith-centric DB usage to a more specialized architecture (Gitaly + PgBouncer + sharded Postgres) is a textbook example of splitting responsibilities and scaling horizontally. The strategy is less about clever queries and more about architecture: isolate, pool, and distribute.
keyTakeaways: Isolate heavy workloads (Git RPCs) from your web app — specialized services (Gitaly) can be scaled independently.
Use connection pooling (PgBouncer) to reduce DB connection churn — this often immediately stabilizes Postgres under web load.
Shard by a stable key and automate routing + failover — sharding increases ops complexity but buys horizontal write scale and lower tail latency.
companyCaseStudy.codeExample:
example: # PgBouncer transaction pooling snippet (postgresql)
[databases]
gitlab = host=pg-shard-1 port=5432 dbname=gitlab user=gitlab

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = md5
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 10000
default_pool_size = 100

# Rails (database.yml) example: connect to pgbouncer
production:
  adapter: postgresql
  host: pgbouncer-host
  port: 6432
  database: gitlab
  pool: 25
  checkout_timeout: 5

concept.title: Bulkhead Pattern: Stop One Failure from Sinking the Whole Ship
concept.summary: The Bulkhead pattern isolates failures by partitioning resources (threads, connections, or memory) so a problem in one area can't exhaust the whole system. It transforms a single blast radius into many small, contained incidents—improving availability and predictability under load.
concept.explanation:
## WHY it matters

Imagine a ship: when one compartment floods, watertight bulkheads keep the rest afloat. In distributed systems, a slow database query, a flapping downstream service, or a CPU-heavy report can behave like floodwater — if it consumes shared threads, connections, or memory it can make the entire service unavailable. The *Bulkhead pattern* is about adding watertight partitions to your app so one overloaded path doesn't sink everything.

### Analogy — the ferry terminal
Think of a ferry terminal with multiple queues: cars, bicycles, and pedestrians. If cars take longer to board, they shouldn't clog the pedestrian lane. Each lane has its own capacity. Bulkheads are those separate lanes.

---

## HOW it works (visual)

Mermaid flowchart showing isolation of resource pools:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Client Request] --> B{Route}
  B -->|Service A| C[Pool A (size N)]
  B -->|Service B| D[Pool B (size M)]
  C --> E[Downstream A]
  D --> F[Downstream B]
  E -.->|Slow/Fail| C
  F -.->|Slow/Fail| D
  style C fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
  style D fill:#9ff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

Sequence showing a request that hits capacity and is rejected fast:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Gateway: Request for heavy job
  Gateway->>PoolA: tryAcquire()
  PoolA-->>Gateway: reject (pool full)
  Gateway-->>Client: 503 / retry-after
```

---

## Practical approaches

- *Thread/worker pool isolation*: give each critical route its own thread pool/executor. Example: database reads vs writes use different pools.
- *Semaphore (concurrency) bulkheads*: limit concurrent executions per dependency without creating new threads — cheaper and simpler in async systems.
- *Connection pool sizing*: cap DB connection usage per service component.
- *Separate processes/containers*: run high-risk components in separate services/hosts.
- *Rate limiting + queues*: combine with throttling or queues to smooth bursts.

### Before / After (quick comparison)

| State | Before (no bulkheads) | After (bulkheaded) |
|-------|------------------------|---------------------|
| Symptom | One slow dependency exhausts thread pool -> cascading timeouts | Problem confined to a partition; other routes continue serving |
| Latency | High tail latency for all endpoints | Only affected endpoints have higher latency |
| Availability | Whole service becomes unhealthy | Partial degradation, better overall uptime |

---

## When to use it

- When a service talks to multiple downstream systems (DBs, queues, APIs) and a slow one can consume shared resources.
- When you need predictable latency under partial failures or bursts.
- When a single request type can tie up expensive resources (file uploads, reports).

Avoid overusing bulkheads for tiny services where added complexity outweighs benefits.

---

## Code examples: patterns you can apply

### 1) Java: semaphore bulkhead (minimal dependency)

```java
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class ExternalServiceClient {
  // allow up to 10 concurrent calls to this downstream
  private final Semaphore sem = new Semaphore(10);

  public String call() throws Exception {
    boolean acquired = sem.tryAcquire();
    if (!acquired) {
      throw new RuntimeException("Bulkhead: too many concurrent calls");
    }
    try {
      // make network call, DB call, etc.
      return doNetworkCall();
    } finally {
      sem.release();
    }
  }
}
```

This quickly rejects excess work instead of letting requests pile up and waiting for timeouts.

### 2) Spring + Resilience4j (thread and semaphore bulkheads)

```java
// configure resilience4j bulkhead in application.yml
resilience4j.bulkhead.instances.myService.maxConcurrentCalls: 20
resilience4j.bulkhead.instances.myService.maxWaitDuration: 0

// usage
Bulkhead bulkhead = bulkheadRegistry.bulkhead("myService");
Supplier<String> decorated = Bulkhead.decorateSupplier(bulkhead, () -> client.call());
Try.ofSupplier(decorated).recover(throwable -> "fallback");
```

### 3) Node.js: separate worker pools using worker threads

```js
// main server delegates heavy work to a worker pool
const { Worker } = require('worker_threads');
// manage pool size and queue, e.g., using 'node-worker-threads-pool'
```

---

## BEFORE / AFTER metrics example

| Metric | Before Bulkheads | After Bulkheads |
|--------|------------------:|----------------:|
| 99th percentile latency | 3s | 600ms |
| Successful requests served (degraded dependency down) | 20% | 85% |
| Mean CPU utilization | 95% (starved) | 70% |

*(Numbers illustrative — actual results vary based on workloads and sizing.)*

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- **Too many tiny compartments**: If you create a bulkhead for every minor path you may underutilize capacity. Group similar workloads sensibly.
- **Wrong sizing**: Too-small bulkheads cause unnecessary rejections; too-large fail to protect. Use load tests and production metrics to tune.
- **Shared underlying resources**: Bulkheads that share memory or a single DB connection pool still risk cascading failure. Ensure isolation covers the actual scarce resources.
- **Ignoring backpressure**: Rejection needs a clear strategy: retries, fallbacks, or user-friendly errors. Blind retries can worsen overload.
- **Complexity creep**: Introduce monitoring and observability early so you can see rejected counts, queue lengths, and live tuning.

---

## Monitoring & operational guidance

Track these metrics per bulkhead:
- concurrentCalls (usage)
- rejectedCalls (how often you hit the limit)
- success/failure rates and latency

Alert on sustained high rejection rates — that signals either a sizing problem or real capacity exhaustion.

---

## Short checklist to implement

1. Identify high-risk paths (slow external calls, CPU-heavy jobs).
2. Choose isolation mechanism (semaphores, thread pools, separate process).
3. Implement graceful rejections with meaningful responses and/or fallbacks.
4. Add metrics and dashboards for bulkhead usage and rejections.
5. Load test and tune sizes.
6. Combine with timeouts, retries with jitter, and rate limiting.

---

## TL;DR
Bulkheads limit the blast radius of failures by partitioning resources. They trade off some concurrency for predictable availability — a powerful trade when parts of your system are brittle or unpredictable.
keyTakeaways: Bulkheads isolate resource usage so a failing/slow subsystem doesn't exhaust the whole service.
Use semaphores, sized thread pools, or separate processes/containers to partition workloads.
Monitor rejection counts and tune sizes; always combine bulkheads with timeouts, sensible retries, and fallbacks.
